content:
**Fixed mrAutoMerge fail-open gate on non-zero requiredReviews (#886)**

**What**: `mrAutoMerge` in both `brain/scripts/vcs/providers/github.mjs:620` and `providers/gitlab.mjs:1178` gated the human-approval refusal on `requiredReviews > 0`. Changed to `requiredReviews !== 0` — only the exact number 0 arms the merge; every other value refuses.

**Why**: A cold review of issue #886's branch measured (with the spawn/fetch seam stubbed and a call-counter) that `null`, `NaN`, and `-1` all evaluate `> 0` as `false`, so the guard fell through and ARMED auto-merge for those inputs — a fail-open gate on a mutating write verb whose entire purpose is "never merge without the review the tier demands". A string `'0'` was already safe under the old check (coerces to 0, `0 > 0` is false) and stays safe under the new one (`'0' !== 0` is true via strict inequality, no coercion).

**Where**: `brain/scripts/vcs/providers/github.mjs`, `brain/scripts/vcs/providers/gitlab.mjs` (the fix); `brain/scripts/vcs/providers/vcs.contract.test.mjs` (new parameterized contract test `only requiredReviews===0 arms — null/NaN/-1/"0" all refuse, seam UNCALLED`, proved RED before the fix); `openspec/changes/issue-886-mr-auto-merge/spec.md` (requirement text rewritten to state exact-zero semantics) and `brain-drafts/vcs-contract.draft.md` (row wording updated, `planAmendment` re-verified unchanged).

**Learned**: The root cause is a classic `>` predicate vs default-parameter semantics gap — `requiredReviews = 1` as a JS default parameter only substitutes for `undefined`, so any explicitly-passed non-number (`null`, `NaN`, a negative, or a string) reaches the comparison as-is, and `X > 0` is a much weaker predicate than "is this exactly the sentinel value that means 'no review required'". For any fail-closed/fail-open boolean gate parameterized by a number that has ONE specific "safe" value, prefer strict equality to that value (`=== 0`) over a magnitude/truthiness comparison — the magnitude comparison silently admits every non-numeric and out-of-range input as "safe" when it isn't. Also worth generalizing: this same class of bug pattern (RE: never-throws holes) showed up in the same PR — `catch (err) { ... err.message ... }` assumed the thrown value was always an `Error`; a `fetchImpl` rejecting with a bare string or `null` broke the pinned key-set / threw a TypeError. Fixed with `err?.message ?? String(err)`, a safe pattern worth reusing anywhere a caught value's type isn't guaranteed.
